title: STATISTICS
body:
Every other course in this degree assumes its inputs are known. This one starts from the opposite
position: you have a sample, the sample is not the truth, and the whole job is saying how far off
you might be and with what confidence. The prerequisite is [[CALCULUS 1]] and it is not decorative,
because a continuous random variable is defined by an [[Integral]] and a probability is an area
under a curve rather than a count of cases.

The course runs in one direction and the dependency is real: describe a sample
([[Descriptive Statistics]]), model the mechanism that produced it ([[Probability]],
[[Random Variable]], [[Probability Distribution]]), work out how a statistic computed from a sample
behaves across all the samples you did not take ([[Sampling Distribution]],
[[Central Limit Theorem]]), and only then make claims ([[Confidence Interval]],
[[Hypothesis Testing]], [[Linear Regression]]). Blocks 4 through 6 are unreadable without block 3,
and block 3 is unreadable without block 2.

**For this vault it is the bridge into the machine learning material.** Block 4's
[[Type I and Type II Errors]] is exactly the [[Confusion Matrix]] that `COMP 4TH YEAR/` uses under
different names, block 5's contingency table is that same $2 \times 2$ grid, and block 6's
regression is the simplest supervised model there is. It also supplies the vocabulary
([[Random Variable]], expectation, [[Probability Distribution]]) that [[Entropy]] and
[[KL Divergence]] are functions of.

## Topics

### Exploratory data analysis and descriptive statistics

- [[Descriptive Statistics]]: what you do before any inference. Data classification (qualitative,
  quantitative, discrete, continuous), what each graphical display is for (histogram, frequency
  polygon, stem-and-leaf, boxplot), and **the sample-versus-population distinction that every
  later formula depends on**
- [[Average Value]]: Evan's index into the three measures of central tendency, and the question of
  which one to report
- [[Mean]]: the arithmetic average, $\bar{x}$ for a sample and $\mu$ for a population, and the one
  weakness that motivates the other two
- [[Median]]: the robust middle, and why skewed data wants it
- [[Mode]]: the most frequent value, and the only summary that works on qualitative data
- [[Variance]]: spread. Variance and standard deviation as one topic, the interquartile range as
  the robust alternative, and **why the sample formula divides by $n-1$**

### Foundations of probability theory

- [[Probability]]: sample spaces, events as [[Sets|sets]], the three axioms, and counting
  outcomes with [[Permutation]] and [[Combination]] from [[DISCRETE MATH]]
- [[Conditional Probability]]: $P(A \mid B)$, the multiplication rule, and independence defined
  rather than assumed
- [[Bayes Theorem]]: inverting a conditional. The formula, base rates, and the medical test that
  is positive and probably still wrong
- [[Random Variable]]: attaching a number to an outcome, discrete versus continuous, and the two
  summaries that follow ($E[X]$ and $\text{Var}(X)$)
- [[Probability Distribution]]: **the family-selection table.** Binomial, Poisson, and geometric on
  the discrete side, uniform, exponential, and normal on the continuous side, each with the
  question it answers
- [[Bernoulli Distribution]]: a single trial, the atom the binomial is built from
- [[Probability Density Function]]: PDFs and CDFs, why $P(X = x) = 0$ for a continuous variable,
  and why a density has to integrate to $1$
- [[Normal Distribution]]: the bell curve, standardising to $z$, and the 68-95-99.7 rule

### Sampling distributions and inference

- [[Sampling Distribution]]: the distribution of a *statistic* rather than of the data, standard
  error, and what makes an estimator biased
- [[Central Limit Theorem]]: sample means go normal as $n$ grows **whatever the population looks
  like**. The single result that makes the rest of the course possible
- [[Confidence Interval]]: $z$- and $t$-intervals for a mean and for a proportion, what drives the
  width, and the interpretation almost everyone gets wrong

### Hypothesis testing

- [[Hypothesis Testing]]: the hub. $H_0$ and $H_1$, the test statistic, the significance level
  $\alpha$, one-sample and two-sample tests, and independent versus paired designs
- [[P-VALUES]]: the probability of data this extreme *given the null*, and the three things it is
  not
- [[Type I and Type II Errors]]: false positives at rate $\alpha$, false negatives at rate $\beta$,
  power $1 - \beta$, and the trade-off you cannot escape. **The note the whole
  [[Confusion Matrix]] set in `COMP 4TH YEAR/` hangs from**

### Categorical data and structural modelling

- [[Chi-Square Test]]: goodness of fit against a claimed distribution, and contingency tables for
  independence between two categorical variables
- [[ANOVA]]: comparing three or more means at once without inflating $\alpha$, the $F$-statistic as
  a ratio of variances, and the sums-of-squares decomposition

### Linear regression and correlation

- [[Linear Regression]]: scatter diagrams, the least squares line $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$, and
  residuals. **The same object as [[Least Squares]] in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]]**,
  derived by calculus here and by [[Projection]] there
- [[Correlation]]: Pearson's $r$, the coefficient of determination $r^2$, and the standing warning
  that neither one is causation

## Core Facts to Know

- **A statistic is computed from a sample; a parameter describes the population.** $\bar{x}$
  estimates $\mu$, $s$ estimates $\sigma$, $\hat{p}$ estimates $p$. Roman letters for what you
  measured, Greek for what you want.
- Mean, median, and mode coincide on a symmetric distribution and separate on a skewed one. On
  right-skewed data $\text{mode} < \text{median} < \text{mean}$, because the [[Mean]] follows the
  tail.
- The [[Mean]] is the only one of the three that uses every value, which is both why it is
  efficient and why one outlier moves it.
- **Sample variance divides by $n - 1$, not $n$.** Deviations are taken from $\bar{x}$ rather than
  the unknown $\mu$, which makes them too small; $n - 1$ is the degrees of freedom left over and
  the correction that makes $s^2$ unbiased.
- $s = \sqrt{s^2}$ has the units of the data, $s^2$ does not. Report the standard deviation, do
  algebra with the variance.
- The three probability axioms: $P(A) \geq 0$, $P(S) = 1$, and $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$ for
  disjoint $A$ and $B$. Everything else is derived, including $P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$.
- **Mutually exclusive and independent are different and nearly opposite.** Disjoint events with
  non-zero probability are maximally *dependent*: knowing $A$ happened tells you $B$ did not.
- $P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B)/P(B)$, so $P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)P(B)$. Independence is exactly
  $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$.
- **Bayes: $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(B \mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}$.** The posterior is the likelihood times
  the prior, normalised. A rare condition plus an accurate test still gives mostly false positives,
  and that is the base rate at work, not a flaw in the test.
- $E[X] = \sum x_i P(x_i)$ for discrete, $\int x f(x)\,dx$ for continuous. Expectation is linear
  always: $E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b$, with no independence needed.
- $\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$, and $\text{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\text{Var}(X)$. Adding a
  constant shifts the mean and leaves the spread alone.
- $\text{Var}(X + Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y)$ **only when $X$ and $Y$ are independent.**
  Variances add, standard deviations do not.
- Binomial for a fixed number of trials, Poisson for events in an interval, geometric for the wait
  until the first success. Exponential is the geometric's continuous twin.
- Binomial: $\mu = np$, $\sigma^2 = np(1-p)$. Poisson: $\mu = \sigma^2 = \lambda$, which is the
  fact that identifies it.
- **For a continuous variable $P(X = x) = 0$.** A density is not a probability; only its integral
  over an interval is, which is why $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx = 1$ and why $<$ versus $\leq$
  stops mattering.
- The CDF $F(x) = P(X \leq x)$ is the antiderivative of the PDF, so $f = F'$ and
  $P(a < X < b) = F(b) - F(a)$. Every table lookup you ever do is a CDF.
- $z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$ turns any normal into the standard normal. **All normal tables are
  one table.**
- 68-95-99.7 within one, two, and three standard deviations. Beyond three is roughly $1$ in $370$,
  which is why "three sigma" is used as a synonym for surprising.
- **Central limit theorem: $\bar{X}$ is approximately normal with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation
  $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$, whatever the population distribution.** $n \geq 30$ is the usual rule of thumb,
  smaller if the population is already symmetric.
- **The standard error is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$, so precision costs quadratically.** Halving the error
  bar takes four times the data. This is the most practically useful formula in the course.
- Use $z$ when $\sigma$ is known, $t$ when it is estimated by $s$. The $t$ distribution is fatter
  tailed, indexed by $n - 1$ degrees of freedom, and converges to $z$ as $n$ grows.
- **"95% confident" is a statement about the procedure, not about this interval.** 95% of intervals
  built this way contain $\mu$; this particular one either does or does not, and it is not a 95%
  probability that $\mu$ is inside it.
- $H_0$ is the claim of no effect and it is the one being tested. You **reject** it or **fail to
  reject** it, and you never accept it. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
- $\alpha$ is chosen before you look at the data. A $p$-value is compared against it and the
  comparison is the whole decision: $p < \alpha$ rejects.
- **A $p$-value is $P(\text{data this extreme} \mid H_0)$.** It is not $P(H_0 \mid \text{data})$,
  not the probability you are wrong, and not a measure of effect size.
- **Type I is rejecting a true $H_0$ (false positive, rate $\alpha$); Type II is failing to reject
  a false one (false negative, rate $\beta$).** Lowering $\alpha$ raises $\beta$ for fixed $n$;
  the only way to buy down both is more data.
- Power is $1 - \beta$, the probability of catching a real effect. It is the same quantity
  [[Sensitivity|recall]] measures in a classifier.
- $\chi^2 = \sum \dfrac{(O - E)^2}{E}$, summing over cells. Goodness of fit compares one variable
  against a claimed distribution; a contingency table tests two variables for independence, with
  $E_{ij} = \text{(row total)}\times\text{(column total)}/n$.
- **A $2 \times 2$ contingency table and a binary [[Confusion Matrix]] are the same object.** One
  is tested for independence, the other is summarised into rates, and the four cells are the same
  four counts.
- ANOVA tests $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \cdots = \mu_k$ with one test rather than $\binom{k}{2}$
  pairwise ones, which would inflate the family-wise error rate. $F = \text{MS}_{\text{between}} /
  \text{MS}_{\text{within}}$, and $\text{SS}_{\text{total}} = \text{SS}_{\text{between}} +
  \text{SS}_{\text{within}}$.
- **Least squares minimises $\sum(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$**, giving $\beta_1 = r\,(s_y/s_x)$ and
  $\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \beta_1\bar{x}$. The line always passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$.
- Residuals sum to zero and are uncorrelated with $x$ by construction, so **a pattern in a residual
  plot means the model is wrong**, not merely imprecise.
- $-1 \leq r \leq 1$, $r$ measures **linear** association only, and $r^2$ is the proportion of
  variance in $y$ the line accounts for. A perfect parabola through the origin can have $r = 0$.
- **Correlation is not causation, and it is not the only thing $r$ misses**: it is destroyed by
  non-linearity, inflated by outliers, and can be manufactured or reversed by aggregating groups.

## Related courses

- [[DISCRETE MATH]] (MATH 1271) supplies block 2 whole. Events are [[Sets]], the axioms are stated
  on sets, Venn diagrams are that note's material, and [[Permutation]] and [[Combination]] are how
  you count the outcomes in the numerator. This course links them rather than restating them.
- [[CALCULUS 1]] is the stated prerequisite and it is where continuous random variables come from:
  a density is a function, a probability is an [[Integral]] of it, and the CDF is its
  antiderivative. [[CALCULUS 2]]'s integration techniques are what actually evaluate the
  exponential and gamma cases.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] (MATH 2303): **[[Linear Regression]] here and
  [[Least Squares]] there are one object.** Minimising the sum of squared residuals and taking a
  [[Projection]] onto a column space give the identical normal equations, and $r^2$ is Pythagoras
  on the resulting right triangle. Covariance matrices in
  [[Principal Component Analysis|PCA]] are built out of the [[Variance]] defined here.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] and [[ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE]]: this is the statistical floor under both.
  [[Type I and Type II Errors]] is [[False Positive]] and [[False Negative]], power is
  [[Sensitivity]], the true negative rate is [[Specificity]], the contingency table is the
  [[Confusion Matrix]], and stratified sampling is [[Stratification]]. [[Linear Regression]] is the
  simplest supervised model, [[Logistic Regression]] is what you use when the response is a
  [[Binary Classification|binary label]], and [[Gradient Descent]] reaches the same line the normal
  equations reach in closed form.
- [[Information Theory]] and [[Entropy]]: [[Shannon Entropy]] is $-E[\log P(X)]$, an
  **expectation of a [[Random Variable]]**, and [[Cross-Entropy]], [[KL Divergence]], and
  [[Cross-Entropy Loss]] are all functionals of a [[Probability Distribution]]. None of them parse
  without block 2.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631): [[Hashing]] discusses collisions without ever computing
  one. How many keys before a collision is likely is the birthday problem, which is
  [[Probability]] plus [[Combination]], and average-case bucket occupancy is a
  [[Probability Distribution|Poisson]] question.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]]: average-case analysis is an expectation over the input
  distribution, which is why randomised quicksort has an $O(n\log n)$ *expected* time and an
  $O(n^2)$ worst case. [[Random Numbers]] and [[Simulation]] in [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] are how
  you sample a distribution when you cannot integrate it.
- [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] (MATH 4111): classical cryptanalysis is applied frequency statistics, and a
  $\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit test against English letter frequencies is a working key-ranking
  criterion. Modern ciphers are judged by whether their output is distinguishable from
  [[Random Numbers|uniform random]].
- [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] (MATH 3200): the bivariate normal and any joint density need double
  integrals, and the normalising constant of the bell curve is the Gaussian integral, which is
  evaluated by a change to polar coordinates that this course quotes and that one performs.

---

Pointer added 2026-08-16, ahead of this course's own pass: **regression here and [[Least Squares]]
in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] (MATH 2303) are the same object seen twice.** Minimising
the sum of squared residuals and projecting $\mathbf{y}$ onto the column space of $X$ give the
identical normal equations, and $R^2$ is Pythagoras on the resulting right triangle. Both notes
should say so. Discharged by this pass: [[Linear Regression]] now exists and says exactly that.
